extracted.intended_audience: politically-engaged British public and policymakers (18th‑century Parliamentarians and readers of political pamphlets)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the prudence, unity, and conduct of a national administration—especially in matters of colonial taxation, trade regulation, and foreign negotiation. Focuses on what makes an administration effective, honest, and legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of fiscal authority to preserve unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific power of levying money in the colonies must be retained as a 'sacred trust' in the hands of Great Britain; if stripped of this right, 'every principle of unity and subordination in the empire was gone forever.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Losing the power to levy money would render the presiding authority of the empire an empty name; occasional use in exigence is acceptable, but habitual exercise for ordinary supply would extinguish colonial freedom. Policy should be adjusted to human nature rather than abstract legal speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisions founded on full public evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay before Parliament the whole detail of the affairs—'every paper of office', witnesses of merchants, manufacturers, officers—so that ignorance does not mislead deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public presentation of all relevant documents and testimony (civil and military officers, revenue officers, merchants from every town) is necessary to ensure Parliament reaches the right judgment rather than relying on ministerial assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat merchants' testimony as salient practical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants' testimony that debts in America were great, trade was declining, and manufacturers were dismissing workers was necessary to bring the matter home to feeling and to inform Parliamentary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such testimony supplies essential practical detail; contempt for it is inappropriate because if merchants had given the opposite (claiming uninterrupted trade under resistance) they would be rightly distrusted. Use merchants' petitions and thanks as evidence of the effect of measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use policy reversals (e.g., repeal) to restore order and create openings for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeal of the Stamp Act produced expected good effects: 'quiet was restored; trade generally returned; time and means were furnished for better strengthening of government... and for recovering, by judicious measures, the affections of the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When repeal or moderation restores tranquillity, governments should use that respite to strengthen institutions and pursue measures to win public goodwill instead of returning immediately to the condemned policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize trade over small revenue yields
rubrics_metrics.description: In deliberations concerning America, 'to take trade as the primary end, and revenue but as a very subordinate consideration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where trade is likely to suffer, prefer protecting commerce rather than levying taxes whose produce is 'contemptible' relative to the potential harm; revenue measures should be subordinate to trade preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design duties to minimize smuggling by balancing duty and risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold out as few temptations to smuggling as possible, 'by keeping the duties as nearly as they could on a balance with the risk.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust port duties (mode and quantity) with awareness of the collection difficulty and local conditions so as to reduce incentives for clandestine trade and smuggling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply trade regulations targetedly rather than indiscriminately
rubrics_metrics.description: When confining returns to the mother country, apply the remedy 'to that part where the disease existed, and to that only' rather than broad restraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrowly directed regulations likely to check specific harmful clandestine trades (e.g., with Hamburg and Holland) instead of blanket prohibitions that unnecessarily limit colonial commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarge legitimate colonial foreign trade when safe for domestic interests
rubrics_metrics.description: It became our interest to let colonies into as much foreign trade as could be given them 'without interfering with our own', securing returns to the mother country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate colonial trade with foreign plantations and southern Europe where it benefits Britain overall; restrictions should be lifted where they are unfavorable to British advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult broad merchant and manufacturing opinion, not individual favorites
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial regulations should be aided by the opinion of merchants generally, not directed by 'one or two merchants' in private interest or favorites seeking contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold numerous and public meetings with merchants and manufacturers from many towns, hear petitions, and seek wide-based practical knowledge to inform policy; avoid letting private advantage drive national regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer practical testimony and petitions over pamphlet self-referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of political argumentation that continually hands readers 'from one of their own pamphlets to another' instead of appealing to those most affected and best judges of the measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground arguments and policy claims in the petitions, thanks, and evidence of affected parties rather than in a self-referential cycle of partisan tracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue neglected foreign claims vigorously and in concert with claimants
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims like the Manilla ransom and the Canada bills should be actively pursued; neglect by predecessors makes negotiation harder but does not defeat right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revive neglected claims promptly, coordinate with persons interested, reject superficial arbitration when unjust, and press negotiations energetically to secure satisfaction or acceptable settlements in concert with stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take merchants' local expertise into diplomatic negotiation where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: In concluding treaties (e.g., the Russian treaty) the opinion of merchants immediately concerned was taken and gave 'entire and unreserved approbation of every article'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers should consult merchants resident in relevant foreign courts and give due weight to their mature, local practical advice when framing commercial treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek united administration composed of men who trust one another
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of having the great strongholds of government 'in well-united hands'—capital offices of deliberation and execution occupied by those who can 'deliberate with mutual confidence' and execute with 'firmness and fidelity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective administration requires cohesion and mutual trust to secure predominance of right and uniform principles; while not excluding coalitions, avoid unions that carry unreconciled discord and produce weakness and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent moral governance—avoid rewarding some while punishing others
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'in vain to endeavor to check the progress of irreligion and licentiousness, by punishing such crimes in one individual, if others equally culpable are rewarded with the honors and emoluments of the state.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment and reward must be applied consistently; selective enforcement undermines public morals and faith in institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against venality and the gradual corruption of public men
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals may be 'debauched away' from legitimate connections by gradual changes in company and habit—friendship to civility to enmity—so that earlier principles are lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to the subtle, progressive seduction of office: watch for shifts from principle to practical convenience, resist ministerial cant that sanctifies power, and value examples of unshaken adherence to principle rather than opportunistic ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer men of steadiness and principle to mere 'ability' that sacrifices consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'men of ability and virtue' conveys no definite idea—what is required to cure national distrust is men whose principles and personal character can remedy the distemper; men willing to adhere to connections and public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate statesmen not by opportunistic political skill alone but by demonstrated constancy, honor, and the capacity to resist factional temptations; they may forfeit some celebrated 'ability' but preserve public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid resort to military coercion and dangerous commissions in colonial governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of military power and new dangerous commissions over colonies tend to produce disorder and discontents; suspending assemblies and exercising force is suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measures that secure voluntary compliance and legal remedies; military coercion risks renewed disorder and undermines prospects of returning to 'true centre of gravity' unless replaced by conciliatory policy (e.g., ideas of 1766).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use periods of tranquillity to correct previous errors rather than relapse
rubrics_metrics.description: After a period of restored quiet and returned trade, administration should profit from the season of tranquillity rather than return to the condemned measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should take advantage of peace to strengthen government and recover affections of people, rather than squandering the opportunity by reverting to previously harmful schemes.
